current.context: Net::DNS uses a 16-bit query ID to match responses to the corresponding requests.  In versions up to and including 1.57, the ID is obtained from Perl's built-in rand() function.  An attacker that can observe the sequence of query IDs is able to expose the internal state of the PNRG and hence predict query IDs before they are transmitted.  The victim Net::DNS instance is then exposed to forged responses injected by the attacker.  Note that the deduplication cache in 1.57 has no impact on the feasibility of this attack.

An uncontrolled recursion vulnerability exists in the LINE iOS app prior to version 26.19.0.

The Flex Message processing component does not adequately validate the structure of externally supplied message content.

As a result, an attacker who is able to send a crafted message to a victim could cause the application to crash when the message is received or displayed.

A server-side mitigation has been deployed that also protects existing iOS clients that have not been updated to version 26.19.0.

current.context: Connaisseur is an admission controller that integrates container image signature verification into a Kubernetes cluster. Prior to 3.11.1, the Cosign validator counts valid signature layers rather than distinct trust roots for trustRoot: "*" policies using an explicit threshold or an implicit require-all policy. An attacker who controls one configured trust root's signing key and can attach multiple signatures to an image can satisfy a threshold intended to require multiple independent roots, causing admission without the intended signer quorum. Policies using a single trust root or the required option are not affected. This issue is fixed in 3.11.1.

current.context: Aether Project AMF supports termination of NAS signalling, NAS ciphering & integrity protection, registration management, connection management, mobility management, access authentication and authorization, security context management. Prior to 3.1.6, a malformed NGAP PathSwitchRequest can contain a UESecurityCapabilities information element whose extensible APER bit-string representation has no bytes even though decoding reports no error. In ngap/handler.go, HandlePathSwitchRequest checks only whether the element is present before six index-zero reads of its encryption and integrity algorithm fields, causing an unrecovered panic in the NGAP receive goroutine and terminating the AMF. The described attacker is a rogue or compromised gNB on the N2 interface and additionally needs a registered UE's AMF-UE-NGAP-ID; a bare over-the-air UE cannot trigger the issue. This issue is fixed in version 3.1.6.

current.context: ALTCHA is a Go library for creating and verifying ALTCHA challenges. Prior to 2.1.0, parseServerSignature can leave ServerSignatureVerificationData.Extra uninitialized when url.ParseQuery returns partial values and an error for a malformed percent escape in VerificationData. A later write of an unknown parsed key to the nil map panics before VerifyServerSignature or VerifyServerSignatureSafe completes signature verification, so an unauthenticated client can abort a request. Standard net/http recovers the request goroutine, while application goroutines or frameworks without recovery can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 2.1.0.

current.context: CKAN is an open-source data management system for data hubs and data portals. Prior to 2.10.11 and 2.11.6, the web user registration flow authenticates a newly registered account without first regenerating the session identifier when server-side session storage is configured. An attacker who can set a session cookie in a victim's browser or obtain the victim's current valid session identifier can reuse that identifier after the victim registers, gaining access to the new account. CKAN uses cookie-based sessions by default, and web registration is disabled by default through ckan.auth.create_user_via_web. This issue is fixed in CKAN 2.10.11, 2.11.6, and 2.12.0.

current.context: The King Addons for Elementor – 100+ Elementor Widgets, 4 000+ Elementor Templates, WooCommerce Builder, Mega Menu, Popup Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 51.1.89. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. current.context: Etherpad is a real-time collaborative editor. From 1.8.14 until 3.3.3, the pre-authentication /static/* plugin asset handler in src/node/utils/Minify.ts performs a backslash-to-forward-slash conversion after src/node/utils/sanitizePathname.ts has completed its POSIX path checks. On POSIX systems the sanitizer correctly treats backslashes as ordinary filename bytes, but the later conversion turns encoded backslash-separated parent-directory segments into traversal components without revalidation or containment. The expressPreSession registration and the always-present ep_etherpad-lite core pseudo-plugin make this path reachable without credentials, allowing a remote attacker to read any file available to the Etherpad process. Disclosed configuration or environment secrets can expose administrator credentials, after which the administrator plugin installer can provide in-process code execution and full server compromise. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.3.

current.context:
In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `<= 2.0.0-rc8` (and the deprecated v1 module paths `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11 <= 1.6.8`, `github.com/ThalesGroup/crypto11 <= 1.7.0-rc1` and `github.com/ThalesIgnite/crypto11 <= 1.2.5`), the key-pair and certificate lookup functions (`FindKeyPair`, `FindKeyPairs`, `FindKeyPairsWithAttributes`, `FindAllKeyPairs`, the `FindRSAKeyPair*` family and `FindAllPairedCertificates`) pair a private key with a public key object, or with a certificate, by `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` alone, take the first match the token returns, and never verify that it belongs to the private key. PKCS#11 permits a session that has not logged in to create public token objects, so anyone able to open a session on the token — without the PIN — can plant a public key or certificate carrying a victim key's `CKA_ID` and label, and crypto11 may return it as that key's public half. An application that publishes or trusts `Signer.Public()` (a JWKS endpoint, a key registry, `authorized_keys`, a CSR) then publishes the attacker's key, and relying parties accept anything the attacker signs as coming from the service. On the v1 line the lookup also falls back to a class-and-key-type-only search when the private key has no `CKA_ID`, pairing a label-only private key with the first public key of its type on the token.



The v1 module paths are deprecated and will not be fixed; users should migrate to github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2 version 2.0.0-rc9 or later.

current.context: The Toocheke Companion plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Missing Authorization leading to arbitrary post and attachment deletion in versions up to, and including, 2.38. This is due to a missing object-level capability check in the toocheke_tapas_ajax_cleanup_start() and toocheke_tapas_ajax_cleanup_step() AJAX handlers; the toocheke_tapas_cleanup_ajax_guard() method only verifies the primitive delete_posts capability (held by every Contributor) and never calls current_user_can('delete_post', $post_id) or delete_others_posts before passing the attacker-supplied series_post_id to wp_delete_post() and wp_delete_attachment() with force-delete enabled. The required nonce is emitted on the Import: Tapas admin page, which is gated only by edit_posts, so a Contributor can read it. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Contributor-level access and above, to permanently delete any importer-created series post, every child 'comic' post attached to it, and every Media Library attachment belonging to those posts — regardless of which user originally created them.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip.

Every INTEGER or ENUMERATED longer than four content octets reaches os2ip, which iterates over each content octet with $result = ($result * 256) + $octet. Each multiplication operates on a bigint that grows by one octet per step, so decoding an n-octet value takes O(n^2) bigint work. Nothing limits content length before this loop runs.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a single oversized INTEGER or ENUMERATED value.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv.

asn_recv peeks the socket in a loop, doubling the buffer size on each pass until a tag and length can be decoded. An inverted boolean guard ($tb || rather than $tb &&) prevents the need-more-data exit from firing once a tag byte has been decoded. When asn_decode_length returns no value because the length is absent or incomplete, no exit fires for that case either. MSG_PEEK leaves socket data unconsumed, so each re-peek returns at once while the buffer size doubles.

A single truncated BER header sent to a process calling asn_recv doubles the peek buffer until memory is exhausted. Perl's realloc failure is fatal and not catchable with eval.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding.

Binary REAL decoding never bounds-checks the exponent length against the available content. For a minimal one-byte binary REAL, the exponent byte is read from outside the element, making the mantissa length -1. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the mantissa is nearly all of the input that follows the element. The long-form exponent path also omits the extra length octet when sizing the mantissa.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a list of such values, as each mantissa loop iterates over the remaining input. The decoded values are also computed from bytes outside each element.

Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via exponent-notation string in INTEGER encoding.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content.

A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. In the constructed form each zero-length segment copies the rest of the input again, so memory grows with the square of the input size.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a short constructed BIT STRING. The resulting value also contains bytes from adjacent input.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form string decoding.

Any constructed-form string element causes the decoder to recurse on the element's contents. The BER encoding controls nesting depth at four bytes per level, with no bound checked. Perl recursion is heap-allocated, so the process grows without a stack crash.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a small deeply nested constructed string.

current.context: pretix offloads certain processes to background tasks that are run by a different server to avoid HTTP workers being clogged with processes that take longer than a usual web request. The browser periodically polls the server to see if the task is already finished using a UUID-shaped task ID. Once the task is completed, pretix resumes to the next step of the operation based on the result of the task. The system does however not check if the result stems from the correct type of task. Therefore, an attacker can supply the UUID of a task of a different type and pretix will continue with the result from the wrong task. In most cases, this will just result in an error because the return types do not match up, but in some cases this can be abused to extract objects the attacker usually should not see. Specifically, a vector was discovered that allowed to abuse this for unauthorized access to other people's ticket purchases. The attacker can, however, not control which purchases they get access to.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to sysread in asn_read and asn_get.

The length an element declares in its BER header is passed to sysread as the read size. Perl grows the target buffer to that size before reading, so memory is allocated from the declared length, not from the data received. A 6-byte header can declare a length of up to 4GB.

A single header makes the reading process allocate the declared size. Where the allocation fails, perl exits with "Out of memory", which eval cannot catch.

current.context:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding and encoding.

The content of an OBJECT IDENTIFIER or RELATIVE-OID element is passed to unpack "w*" on decode, and the arcs of an OID string to pack "w*" on encode. Perl converts each arc to or from its decimal string in time quadratic in the arc's length, and nothing limits that length.

An attacker who controls the decoded data, or an OID string passed to encode, can exhaust CPU with a single oversized arc.

current.context: The Mail Mint – Email Marketing, Automation & WooCommerce Emails with AI Assistance plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'form_id' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.31.9 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. A crafted form_id value such as `1" onmouseover="alert(1)` still resolves to a valid form ID via FormModel::get()'s %d prepared statement placeholder, allowing the payload to bypass empty/draft early-return guards and reach both the HTML id and hidden input value attribute sinks.

This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. current.context: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

current.context: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

current.context: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When a client application enforces step-up authentication or multi-factor authentication (MFA) via a minimum authentication level, Keycloak fails to apply this requirement to login sessions initiated through the credential reset endpoint. An attacker who possesses a user's initial credentials (such as a password) can navigate from the reset interface back to the standard login form and authenticate without completing the required second factor. This flaw allows an attacker to obtain valid access tokens and gain unauthorized access to protected services without satisfying mandatory security controls.

current.context: The UiChemy – Convert Figma, Prompts and AI Builds to Elementor, Gutenberg and Bricks plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'sections[0][settings][raw_css]' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 5.5.3 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. current.context:
Validating an untrusted ISO 8601 duration string into a timedelta field with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few dozen kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The iso8601_duration_re regular expression used to parse ISO 8601 durations (in pydantic/datetime_parse.py) contains an unescaped ".", which also matches digits. On a string of digits, the repeated groups overlap and the regex engine backtracks in quadratic time.

The issue was fixed in commit 62791e66a9f8f118e465ed760c9e2ede9ae3055e. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into timedelta fields.

Validating an untrusted list into a field constrained with unique_items=True with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few hundred kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The ConstrainedList.unique_items_validator validator (in pydantic/types.py) checks each item against all the following ones. For a list with no duplicates (the common, valid case), this results in a quadratic number of comparisons.

The issue was fixed in commit 6ec75e57f277a820ec583e601167f25fe8dc7c87. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted lists into fields constrained with unique_items=True (using conlist() or Field()).

The fix only applies to lists of builtin scalar types (int, float, str, bytes, bool and None), for which duplicates can be detected in linear time. Lists of other types (e.g. models or dictionaries) are still checked in quadratic time, as their items aren't guaranteed to be hashable: bound their size using the max_items constraint.

Pydantic V2 models are not affected.

current.context:
When extra data is allowed, providing both the alias and the name of an aliased TypedDict or dataclass field makes the unvalidated value (provided under the name) overwrite the validated one (provided under the alias), resulting in validated data not matching the declared type.

Extra items are stored in the same dictionary as the fields (the returned dictionary for TypedDict, the instance __dict__ for dataclasses). As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one. The TypedDict validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/typed_dict.rs) and the dataclass validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/dataclass.rs) share this logic.

The issue was fixed in commit 34491f5328f168f14e3769cd5f0f83c0af0f4778.

Impact: validation bypass, as data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into TypedDict or dataclass types with aliased fields and extra data allowed (with extra='allow', or with the extra_items argument for TypedDict), using Pydantic V2 (up to and including 2.14.1).

Pydantic models (BaseModel) are not affected, as extra data is stored separately from fields.

current.context:
Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

current.context:
Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them. As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact: validation bypass, as extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted JSON data into models allowing extra data (with extra='allow'), with a key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__ (e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=...)], int]), using Pydantic from 2.13.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.2.

Python mode validation isn't affected.

current.context: A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. When processing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) documents that lack a root signature, Keycloak accepts the request as long as any assertion within the document is signed, without verifying its context or placement. An attacker holding a validly signed assertion can embed it into an unsigned logout request for another user, causing Keycloak to accept the forged request and terminate the victim's session.

current.context: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When configured with a database that uses case-insensitive collation, Keycloak resolves realm URLs regardless of letter casing. A remote attacker can exploit this behavior by sending requests with alternate letter casing to bypass upstream reverse proxy access controls that rely on case-sensitive path matching. This issue can expose restricted authentication endpoints intended only for internal access, though Keycloak's internal authentication mechanisms remain intact.

current.context: In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

current.context: When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. A third party who controls data a tool returns, such as a record that an MCP server or a function tool returns from an external system, can use this to make the application download a URL on its local network, or make the model provider read an s3:// object or uploaded file with the application's credentials. Applications are affected when tool results can contain third-party data, message history containing those results is serialized and loaded again (stored history, history a UI adapter holds on the server, or Temporal, DBOS or Prefect durable execution), and the model is one Pydantic AI downloads files for, one that honors force_download, or one whose provider resolves non-HTTP file URLs or uploaded files. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0.

current.context: vulnerability-lookup prior to version 7.1.0 contains two security issues in its web interface. First, the /user/toggle_2fa endpoint accepted HTTP GET requests and disabled the authenticated user's two-factor authentication without requiring password confirmation. Because the state-changing operation was reachable via GET, an attacker with a basic account could embed an image element (or any other GET-triggering markup) in a comment pointing to that endpoint. When a victim with 2FA enabled viewed the comment, their browser silently issued the GET request, disabling the victim's second factor of authentication. No CSRF token was enforced on the GET path, and no password was required to confirm the action. Second, the comment detail page (/comment/<uuid>) rendered unpublished comments to any visitor who possessed the URL, bypassing the moderation workflow that was intended to keep such content hidden until approved. The API correctly restricted access, but the web view did not enforce the same authorization check. The combined effect allows an attacker to degrade a victim's account security (removal of 2FA) through a single page view and to read content that was not yet approved for public release.

current.context:
Flowintel's community data launcher script passes the admin API key as a command-line argument to a child Python helper process. On Unix-like systems, process arguments are readable by all local users via standard tools such as ps or by reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline, allowing any local user to observe the key while the helper process is running.

An attacker with local access to the host can capture the admin API key during the brief window in which the helper process is active. Possession of the key grants full administrative access to the Flowintel REST API, enabling unauthorized creation, modification, or deletion of threat intelligence data, users, roles, and organisations.

Preconditions:
- The victim must invoke the community data import or deletion command (launch.sh -tdc or -dtdc) with the API key supplied as a positional argument.
- The attacker must have a local user account on the same host and be able to observe process listings during the helper execution window.

Impact:
- Disclosure of the Flowintel admin API key to any local user.
- Subsequent full administrative control over the Flowintel instance via its REST API.

Affected: <4.1.0

current.context:
Flowintel's template repository subsystem did not adequately constrain file access to the configured repository base directory. Two related weaknesses existed:

- Repository registration and editing accepted arbitrary local paths without verifying they resolved inside the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH, allowing an authenticated user to point a repository at any readable directory on the host.
- Manifest and template file lookups used normalized (non-canonical) path joins and a startswith-based guard that could be bypassed by symbolic links, permitting reads of files outside the intended repository.

An authenticated user with the ability to add or edit a template repository could therefore cause the application to read and return the contents of arbitrary files readable by the service account, including configuration files, credentials, or other sensitive data.

Affected: Flowintel versions prior to 4.1.0.

This vulnerability allows a malicious certificate authority or an attacker positioned on an unencrypted network to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending oversized or deliberately slow responses. current.context:
FlowIntel contains a resource exhaustion vulnerability in its file-to-note conversion feature. When a user converts an attached CSV or JSON file into a case note, the application renders the data as a Markdown table by padding every row to the maximum column count. A crafted file with a small number of filled cells but a very large number of columns (or keys) causes the application to allocate a quadratic number of padded table cells, potentially exhausting a worker process in memory or CPU.

The same issue affects nested JSON values rendered inside table cells, where pretty-printed indentation further inflates the output size.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to a case in FlowIntel
- Ability to attach and convert a CSV or JSON file to a note

Impact:
- Denial of service: exhaustion of a worker process, potentially disrupting service for other users
- No confidentiality or integrity impact

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

current.context:
flowintel contains a log injection vulnerability in its case history (audit log) subsystem. The case history is stored as a line-delimited file where each line represents a single event attributed to a specific user. User-controlled fields, including user names, event messages, and case titles used during case merging, were written to the history file without sanitizing embedded line separator characters (such as carriage return, line feed, vertical tab, form feed, and Unicode line/paragraph separators).

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify case history entries could embed line separators in these fields. Upon writing, the injected separators would split a single intended entry into multiple lines, each of which the history format interprets as a distinct event. This allows an attacker to forge additional history entries attributed to arbitrary users, corrupting the audit trail and undermining the integrity of case records.

The vulnerability affects the case history append and merge operations. No authentication bypass or privilege escalation is required beyond normal case-management access.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context:
The flowintel Docker build workflow used the GitHub Actions checkout action with default credential persistence, causing the job authentication token to be written into the repository's Git configuration file. This file became part of the Docker build context and could be retained in exported build cache layers, even though Git metadata was stripped from the final runtime image.

An attacker with access to the CI/CD build cache or build environment could extract the persisted token and use it to gain unauthorized access to the private source repository.

Impact:
- Exposure of a valid authentication token to the private repository
- Potential unauthorized read access to source code and repository metadata

Affected versions: flowintel < 4.1.0

current.context:
FlowIntel contains multiple security flaws in its note variable resolution, chatbot API tooling, and AI report generation.

- Note variable references (e.g. cross-case or cross-task lookups) were resolved using the viewing user's privileges rather than the destination case's audience. An authenticated user with access to a shared or imported note could embed references to private cases, causing sensitive case data to be pulled into AI report requests, exports, and MISP sends without the referenced case's audience having granted read access.

- The chatbot API tool permitted the language model to invoke any FlowIntel API endpoint, including administrative routes and state-changing GET operations, without an allow-list or path validation. An attacker who can influence the model's instructions (e.g. via untrusted case content) could induce data modification or access restricted endpoints.

- AI report generation passed the Ollama bearer token and full case content as command-line arguments to a child process, exposing them in the system process table to any local user.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context:
Flowintel disabled TLS certificate verification for all MISP API connections and used unverified SSL contexts for IMAP and SMTP STARTTLS mail connections. This allowed an on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker positioned between Flowintel and its MISP or mail servers to impersonate the remote server and intercept sensitive data.

Affected connections include:
- All MISP HTTPS API calls (event retrieval, attribute search, event creation, connectivity checks, and API validation)
- SMTP STARTTLS connections used for sending email notifications
- IMAP TLS connections used for fetching mail archives and testing connectivity

An attacker who can observe or intercept network traffic between Flowintel and the MISP or mail server could:
- Capture MISP API keys and mail credentials (SMTP/IMAP passwords)
- Read all threat intelligence data exchanged (events, attributes, objects, reports)
- Inject or modify threat intelligence data returned to Flowintel

The vulnerability required no authentication on the part of the attacker and no user interaction; it was exploitable by any party with a network position between Flowintel and its configured MISP or mail endpoints.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context:
FlowIntel contained a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability affecting fourteen web routes that performed destructive or state-changing operations. The affected routes accepted HTTP GET requests in addition to (or instead of) POST, which bypassed the Flask-WTF CSRF token validation that is only enforced on non-GET requests.

The vulnerable operations included:
- Case deletion and case merging
- Organisation removal from a case
- Task deletion (case and template)
- Case template and note template deletion
- Connector, connector instance, and icon deletion
- Custom tag deletion and status change
- Taxonomy and galaxy status changes

An attacker who could induce an authenticated user to follow a crafted link or load a page containing a cross-site navigation (e.g., an image tag or redirect) could trigger any of these destructive actions using the victim's session cookie, without the victim's explicit consent or awareness. No special privileges beyond a valid authenticated session with the appropriate role (editor or admin) were required on the victim's account.

Security impact: unauthorized deletion or modification of cases, tasks, templates, connectors, icons, custom tags, taxonomies, and galaxies belonging to the victim or the organisation, resulting in loss of data integrity.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

current.context:
Flowintel , contained a session management vulnerability in its browser authentication mechanism. The session identifier used a bare numeric user ID rather than a credential-bound token, resulting in several related weaknesses:

- Remembered logins (remember-me cookies) remained valid after a user changed their password, allowing an attacker holding a previously issued cookie to retain access indefinitely.
- Server-side session identifiers were not rotated upon login (local, SSO, or remembered), enabling session fixation.
- Self-service email and password changes did not require verification of the current password, permitting an attacker with an active session to modify account credentials without knowledge of the existing password.
- Administrator-initiated password resets did not revoke other browser sessions, invalidate remembered logins, or rotate the affected user's API key.

An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (e.g., through XSS, network interception, or cookie theft) could maintain unauthorized access even after the legitimate user changed their password. Additionally, an attacker with any valid session could change the account's email address or password without knowing the current credentials, effectively taking over the account.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context:
Flowintel contains a privilege escalation vulnerability in its Matrix relay (bot) integration. When the relay forwarded API requests on behalf of a represented user, the authorization and permission checks evaluated the relay bot's elevated role while the request handlers acted as the lower-privileged represented user. This mismatch allowed users with restricted roles (e.g., Read Only) to perform write operations, directory lookups, calendar modifications, assignment changes, template creation, and import actions they were not authorized to perform.

Additionally, relay authority was determined by matching editable user profile fields (name and email) rather than a protected, non-spoofable identifier. An ordinary user who modified their profile to match the expected bot name could be recognized as the trusted relay, enabling impersonation of the bot and potential access to its elevated privileges.

Preconditions:
- A valid Flowintel user account with a restricted role (e.g., Read Only)
- Access to the Matrix relay integration or the ability to send API requests with the relay's API key and a MATRIX-ID header
- For the impersonation vector: ability to edit one's own profile name fields

Security impact:
- Unauthorized write operations by users with read-only or otherwise restricted permissions
- Potential impersonation of the trusted relay bot by ordinary users
- Bypass of organization-level access controls and role-based restrictions
- Unauthorized modification of cases, tasks, calendar events, templates, and user directory entries

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0

current.context:
Flowintel contains multiple SSO identity and organisation trust boundary violations that collectively allow account takeover, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to private case data.

- Keycloak SSO accepted unverified email claims, and all SSO providers (Keycloak, Entra ID, SimpleSAML) could resolve a claimed email address to an existing account that was created via a different sign-in method, enabling cross-provider account collision and unauthorized access to another user's account and data.

- Entra ID role mapping relied on group display names, which tenant members could duplicate by creating a group with the same name as a privileged group (e.g. FlowintelAdmin), resulting in unauthorized role escalation.

- SSO provisioning reused organisations whose display names matched user-controlled profile names, granting the new SSO user access to that organisation's private cases without explicit administrator assignment.

- Case sharing via the API resolved organisations by name using a first-match query, so ambiguous names could silently resolve to the wrong organisation.

Preconditions: an attacker must have a valid SSO identity (Keycloak, Entra ID, or SimpleSAML) or be a member of the relevant Entra tenant. No local administrator access is required.

Security impact: unauthorized access to private case data, privilege escalation to Editor or higher roles, and account takeover across authentication providers.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context:
FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its user directory and assignment endpoints that allows authenticated users to access data belonging to other organisations.

When the LIMIT_USER_VIEW_TO_ORG setting is enabled to restrict directory visibility to the caller's organisation, several API endpoints (user lookup by ID, last name, Matrix ID, and role-based listings) did not consistently enforce the organisation boundary. An authenticated non-admin user could retrieve profiles of users in other organisations by supplying their identifiers.

Additionally, OrgAdmin users could retrieve the task assignments of any user in the system, including tasks and case titles from private cases to which they had no access. The assignment endpoints did not verify that the requested user belonged to the caller's organisation or that the underlying cases were visible to the caller.

Security impact:
- Exposure of user identities (names, Matrix IDs, roles) across organisation boundaries
- Disclosure of task assignments, case titles, and workflow details from private cases
- Potential enumeration of other organisations' membership and case activity

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

current.context:
FlowIntel contains multiple authorization and credential management vulnerabilities affecting connector instances, MISP helper tools, and case templates.

- Connector instance metadata, connectivity checks, and case listings accepted instance IDs without verifying if the acting user had visibility or ownership rights, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive configuration and data.
- Case template serialization and creation processes exposed connector instances attached to templates regardless of the user's permissions, potentially leaking credentials or instance details to users who should not have access.
- Editing connector instances allowed changes to URLs or sharing scopes without requiring re-authentication of API keys, enabling the reuse of another user's credentials in a new context or the leakage of shared keys to unauthorized endpoints.
- Outbound MISP connector keys were incorrectly accepted for authenticating incoming alerts, bypassing the intended separation between outbound integration credentials and inbound alert source authentication.

These issues allow authenticated users to access unauthorized connector data, manipulate credential scopes, and potentially exploit credential confusion between different security contexts.

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

current.context:
flowintel contains multiple authorization bypass vulnerabilities in its Analyzer (MISP Modules) functionality, affecting both the web interface and the REST API.

- Saving analyzer results to a case or task accepted caller-supplied case and task identifiers without verifying that the authenticated user is a member of the target case or holds the required restricted-task permissions. An authenticated user could write notes, create tasks, and attach MISP objects or attributes into another organization's case.

- Stored analyzer results were retrievable by UUID by any authenticated user. Both the web endpoint and the API endpoint returned the full result payload without checking ownership, exposing another user's analysis output.

- The save handler did not validate the structure of the request, did not reject conflicting destination selections, and did not halt processing when a task-note operation failed, allowing partial or unintended writes.

Preconditions: the attacker must possess a valid authenticated session (or API token) in flowintel. No administrative role is required.

Security impact: unauthorized cross-tenant data disclosure (analyzer results) and unauthorized cross-tenant data modification (notes, tasks, MISP objects/attributes in another organization's case).

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context:
flowintel contains an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability affecting multiple endpoints that manage child records of cases and tasks. An authenticated user with access to one case or task could read or modify records belonging to other cases by supplying identifiers of those records directly in the request.

Affected operations include:
- Reading task notes, subtasks, and URL tools by referencing their IDs without verifying they belong to the authorized task
- Retrieving task assignees for a task belonging to a different case
- Editing or deleting timeline events and timeline event links belonging to another case
- Editing or removing case connectors belonging to another case
- Invoking connector module operations (MISP, generic connectors, worker calls) by combining an authorized case with a connector link from a different case

The root cause is that the application authorized the parent resource (case or task) in the URL but then fetched or operated on the child record independently without verifying the child's ownership relationship to the authorized parent.

Security impact: an authenticated user can exfiltrate sensitive threat intelligence data from cases they do not have access to, and can modify or delete timeline entries, connector configurations, and other records in unauthorized cases, leading to data integrity loss and potential disruption of incident response workflows.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0

current.context:
flowintel contains multiple related flaws that allow an authenticated attacker to inject arbitrary HTML or script into pages viewed by other users.

- Timeline rendering: the timeline library's autolinking feature rewrote already-sanitised case notes and imported MISP attribute values into generated HTML link elements. Crafted text containing quote characters could break out of the generated attribute context, altering the surrounding markup and enabling script execution in the victim's browser.

- Search highlighting: the highlight injection logic used a regular expression to locate text between angle brackets and spliced <mark> elements into the resulting string. Because the pattern could match inside HTML attribute values, the rewrite could corrupt or inject content into attributes of already-sanitised markup, again leading to DOM-based cross-site scripting.

- Content-Type confusion: three analyser selection endpoints returned session-stored JSON strings with a text/html content type. A browser receiving such a response will parse and render the body as HTML, so any HTML or script embedded in the stored value is executed in the victim's context.

Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated user with the ability to create or import case content (notes, MISP attributes) containing specially crafted quote or angle-bracket sequences. The victim must subsequently open the affected case timeline, run a search, or request one of the selection endpoints.

Impact: successful exploitation yields DOM-based cross-site scripting in the victim's browser session, potentially allowing disclosure of case data, session manipulation, or execution of arbitrary actions under the victim's identity.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

- Content-Type confusion: three analyser selection endpoints returned session-stored JSON strings with a text/html content type. A browser receiving such a response will parse and render the body as HTML, so any HTML or script embedded in the stored value is executed in the victim's context.

Preconditions: the attacker must be an authenticated user with the ability to create or import case content (notes, MISP attributes) containing specially crafted quote or angle-bracket sequences. The victim must subsequently open the affected case timeline, run a search, or request one of the selection endpoints.

Impact: successful exploitation yields DOM-based cross-site scripting in the victim's browser session, potentially allowing disclosure of case data, session manipulation, or execution of arbitrary actions under the victim's identity.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

current.context: Reposilite is lightweight and easy-to-use repository management software dedicated to Maven-based artifacts in the JVM ecosystem. From 3.5.16 until 3.6.0, as stated by the advisory, the Maven directory-index page interpolates the request URI without HTML escaping in its title, heading, base URL, and parent-directory link. The advisory says the content-embedded ctx.uri() is percent-encoded, preventing tag injection, but that a single quote passes through and breaks the quoted Parent-Directory link; it also says Location.of strips single quotes, so the reachability of the described quote-based trigger remains unresolved. The listing shares the Admin UI origin and does not set the sandbox Content-Security-Policy used for artifact and Javadoc responses, so the reported script execution could access a user's local-storage token. A manager token could enable full instance compromise. The advisory reports version 3.6.0 as fixed.

current.context: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java accumulates attacker-controlled Binary HTTP variable-length integers into the int offset sumBytes. BinaryHttpParser.readRequestHead, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine, and BinaryHttpParser.getIndeterminateLength can narrow long lengths into that offset, causing integer wraparound before buffer indices are calculated. A remote peer that supplies a valid large encoded length to BinaryHttpParser or BinaryHttpDecoder can trigger an unchecked bounds exception from a small malformed message, fail or close the channel, and repeatedly cause denial of service. Java and Netty bounds checks prevent memory corruption, and no information disclosure was observed. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

In Splunk Enterprise for Windows versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a user that holds a role with the edit_user capability could create multiple user accounts that share the same user directory. This could expose user-specific configuration between those accounts, let one account modify configuration used by another account, or disrupt features that depend on separate user directories.
The vulnerability is caused by improper validation of usernames before Splunk Enterprise performs Windows filesystem operations. Windows removes trailing periods from directory names, so distinct usernames can resolve to the same user directory.

current.context: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the earlier CVE-2026-67429 remediation applied validate_path_with_env_config() to only a hand-picked set of file-writing modules, leaving data.csv.write in src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py, data.json_to_csv in src/core/modules/atomic/data/json_to_csv.py, file.copy in src/core/modules/atomic/file/copy.py, and file.move in src/core/modules/atomic/file/move.py outside the FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement boundary. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

current.context: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf in src/core/utils.py resolves and checks a hostname but returns the hostname URL rather than the validated address, and session.get in http.get performs an independent DNS lookup when connecting. A low-privileged caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make the first lookup return a public address and the connection-time lookup return an internal address, bypassing the SSRF guard for all modules that call it and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. Successful exploitation requires attacker-controlled DNS and a successful timing-dependent answer change between the two lookups. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

current.context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure

assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree.  Where the copy reaches a
shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(),
fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then
allocates the copy of the node after it.  The memcpy() leaves the new
shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second
allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new
tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on
the old node's back pointer fires.

Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing
the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated.  A copied shortcut

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure

assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree.  Where the copy reaches a
shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(),
fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then
allocates the copy of the node after it.  The memcpy() leaves the new
shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second
allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new
tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on
the old node's back pointer fires.

the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated.  A copied shortcut
is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there
to follow it.  Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the
trees gc builds are the same as before.

Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation
fail in turn.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA

Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA
space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is
problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to
the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and
report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up
losing dirties.

Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen
ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was
expecting.

Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery

When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area,
write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If
the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is
written, with i_xattr_nid of 0.

Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose
i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node.
f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and
f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps
the stale xattr node:

 - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in
   xattr space after end of list".
 - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area,
   its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs
   come back after recovery.

When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has,
release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block
address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still
be dirty.

f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() fails

Our consistency stress test (fsstress + fio + atomic write workers +
"f2fs_io shutdown 1") triggers below kernel BUG:

 F2FS-fs (vdd): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 0
 ------------[ cut here ]------------
 kernel BUG at fs/f2fs/segment.c:3989!
 Oops: invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
 Workqueue: writeback wb_workfn (flush-253:48)
 RIP: 0010:f2fs_allocate_data_block+0x257a/0x38e0
 Call Trace:
  <TASK>
  do_write_block+0x155/0xc10
  f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340
  f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880
  f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0
  f2fs_write_cache_pages+0x973/0x1f20
  __f2fs_write_data_pages+0x6c4/0x1890
  do_writepages+0x21e/0x560
  __writeback_single_inode+0x119/0x11b0
  writeback_sb_inodes+0x67d/0x17a0
  wb_writeback+0x207/0x820
  wb_workfn+0x128/0xc30
  process_one_work+0x925/0x1600
  worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0
  kthread+0x35f/0x460
  ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0
  ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30
  </TASK>

The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi))
in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512.

The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown
as below:

Thread A (commit atomic write)  Thread B (shutdown)        Thread C (writeback)
- f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write
 - f2fs_commit_atomic_write
  - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write
   - __replace_atomic_write_block
    - f2fs_replace_block
     - __f2fs_replace_block
                                - f2fs_ioc_shutdown
                                 - f2fs_do_shutdown
                                 : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC
                                  - f2fs_sync_fs
                                                           - f2fs_write_single_data_page
                                                           : pass f2fs_cp_error() check
                                  - f2fs_stop_checkpoint
                                  : set CP_ERROR_FLAG
      - change_curseg
       - reset_curseg
       : curseg->segno = new_segno
       : curseg->alloc_type = SSR
       : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff()
         which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free
         slot in new_segno
       - f2fs_get_sum_cache
       : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error()
      : return error w/o restoring curseg
     : goto out_unlock, skip restoring
       old segno, blkoff and alloc_type
                                                            - f2fs_do_write_data_page
                                                             - f2fs_outplace_write_data
                                                              - do_write_block
                                                               - f2fs_allocate_data_block
                                                               : curseg->segno is valid
                                                               : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >=
                                                                 BLKS_PER_SEG)

Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of
f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg
has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left
in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no
free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore
it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG.
Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and
sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang
in D state.

Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no
checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via
reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC,
then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg
instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error
since CP_ERROR_FLA
---truncated---

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute

Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the
admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during
connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set,
then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the
socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock.  Once the
reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer.

Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during
error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock.
Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock
and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed
in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips
mutex_destroy().

Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock
under the same lock.  The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the
lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the
bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the
lock.  To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now
owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and
only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while
a sysfs attribute read is still in progress.  The queue count is
computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original
connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects
may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs

Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list
of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to
lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that.

Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the
the vcpu so that we are sure it is in a quiescent state, and the state be
safely manipulated.

Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack

sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy
lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone,
and nothing compares either length against that allocation.

sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which
added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties
each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the
allocation, which is the half this adds.

Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the
first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers,
so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is
enough; the filesystem does not have to be used.

Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches
differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small
overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error

After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written.
If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR,
and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT.

f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it
as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only
advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes,
about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a
power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount
on the file.

Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing
after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still
reported as -ENOENT.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone

In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds
any underlying queue limits:
1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This
   limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and
   device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS
   writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges
   contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without
   checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM
   target enforces a smaller limit.
2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment
   limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the
   128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages
   are discontiguous.
3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs,
   section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never
   spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors.

Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split()
submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head
half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail
bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head:

  dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048
  != wp_offset 248, len 248

The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing
f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only:

nvd.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone

In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds
any underlying queue limits:
1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This
   limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and
   device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS
   writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges
   contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without
   checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM
   target enforces a smaller limit.
2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment
   limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the
   128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages
   are discontiguous.
3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs,
   section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never
   spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors.

Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split()
submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head
half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail
bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head:

  dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048
  != wp_offset 248, len 248

The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing
f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue

Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons
only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool.
The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one
station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the
drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single
client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page
count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there
for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit
queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for
anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon
valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers.

Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the
measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on
the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its
access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded
by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at
the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery

In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to
TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is
asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so
frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's
mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside
the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of
1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues
behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds
after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore,
and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll
("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The
AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and
only a reboot recovers.

mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets
IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one
station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing
unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with
the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1
("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else
leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the
usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets
the backlog build up.

On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven
through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU
and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with
it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set

The owner of a memfd sealed with F_SEAL_EXEC can still change its
execute bits by setting a POSIX access ACL. With CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL,
this lets an unprivileged owner make a non-executable memfd executable,
bypassing vm.memfd_noexec=2.

simple_set_acl() updates i_mode directly, bypassing the seal check in
shmem_setattr(). Add shmem_set_acl() to check the resulting mode. Share
the F_SEAL_EXEC check with shmem_setattr() using memfd_check_seals_mode()
in include/linux/memfd.h.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: use common helper; simplify description ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings

find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that
are not CoW mappings, which is wrong.

If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have
VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE.

While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires
VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon()
still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma.

This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such
that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that
actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would
require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first
place.

copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared
PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are
shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function
with shareable page tables is the real issue.

If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it
might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant
locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and
possibly freed after calling:

	dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz);

To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a
safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never
end up messing with shared PMD tables in there.

Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd
operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an
anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma.

As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and
also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well
directly for consistency.

A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma)
lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of
VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on
CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004

cros_usbpd_notify_probe_acpi() takes the EC device pointer from
dev_get_drvdata(dev->parent) and assumes it is a struct cros_ec_device.
That only holds when GOOG0003 is a child of GOOG0004. On older devices
without that hierarchy, such as Google Nami, GOOG0003 and GOOG0004 are
siblings under the ACPI EC (PNP0C09):

  PNP0C09:00 (acpi-ec)
  |-- GOOG0003:00 (cros-usbpd-notify-acpi)
  `-- GOOG0004:00 (cros_ec_lpcs)

Before commit db65a06d10b3 ("ACPI: EC: Convert the driver to a platform
one") the parent platform device had no driver data, so the driver
warned and continued without an EC pointer, as intended for these
devices. Since that commit the ACPI EC driver stores its struct acpi_ec
there, so the driver treats a struct acpi_ec as a struct cros_ec_device
and calls cros_ec_cmd() on it for every USB-C PD host event. Plugging
or unplugging a charger then intermittently oopses, followed by soft
lockups and a hung system:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff9cf03220
  #PF: supervisor write access in kernel mode
  Hardware name: Google Nami/Nami, BIOS  09/19/2019
  Workqueue: kacpi_notify acpi_os_execute_deferred
  RIP: 0010:native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath+0x29d/0x330
  Call Trace:
   _raw_spin_lock_irqsave+0x59/0x80
   __mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x129/0x930
   cros_ec_cmd_xfer+0x2a/0xf0 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_ec_cmd_xfer_status+0x1a/0x90 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_ec_cmd+0xb7/0x140 [cros_ec_proto]
   cros_usbpd_get_event_and_notify+0x42/0xc0 [cros_usbpd_notify]
   acpi_ev_notify_dispatch+0x4e/0x70
   acpi_os_execute_deferred+0x1a/0x30

Only read the parent's driver data when the parent's ACPI node is
GOOG0004, and otherwise continue without an EC pointer. While at it,
drop the reference taken by fwnode_get_parent().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained
control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can
therefore access the socket after it has been freed.

Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use
sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA
ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it
is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers.

Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration
so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: hold shkey across socket migration

sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the
new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops
the skb-owned shared-key reference.

If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the
final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the
freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference.

Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release
it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected
authentication key throughout the ownership transfer.

Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and
validated by Trail of Bits.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort()

gmem_abort() maps at s2fd->fault_ipa, which HPFAR_EL2 holds at 4K
granularity whatever the page size. The generic page-table code aligns
it, but pkvm_pgtable_stage2_map() looks up existing mappings over
[addr, addr + size), so on a pKVM host with pages larger than 4K a
guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can
find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault
forever.

The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested
guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one
kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on.

Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as
user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault
exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd
memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.
